Mr. Chairman, in order to understand a little the circumstances in which that speech was delivered

at that time, the hon. minister was presenting a motion for second reading of Bill No. C-102, on banks and banking. We were discussing the motion for second reading of the bill and we know that, at that stage, each of the members may speak once but he cannot reply, let us say to the minister introducing the bill. Moreover, according to another section of the rules, whenever the member introducing a bill rises at a given moment to give an answer to those who asked questions, the debate is then automatically concluded.
Besides, when the former minister of finance, the present member for Davenport, delivered that speech-I regret his absence in the house at this time since I intend to
March 14, 1967

He delivered this speech on Social Credit theories knowing quite well that, according to standing orders, nobody could answer him, the debate being concluded, and that, in short, under the standing orders, no member could rise and refute that speech.
Here are some excerpts from that speech which I would like to comment.
First of all, the Minister without Portfolio, the former minister of finance, starts out from principles which are not really social credit principles. The leitmotiv, the argument used over and over again in that speech of the former minister of finance-which can be found at page 2373 of Hansard for June 14, 1965-the ever-recurring idea is this: the Social Crediters want an inordinate increase in the money supply.
Well, then, Mr. Chairman, objection must be taken immediately to what the former minister of finance wants to include in a theory, when that is not in it at all.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
The point, Mr. Chairman, is not to increase the money supply beyond measure, far from it. What Social Crediters propose is to increase the money supply at the same pace- neither faster nor slower-as, Canadian citizens and Canadian industries are able to increase the Canadian output.
If there is a large increase in Canadian production, there has to be a corresponding increase in the money supply, because the money supply enables Canadian citizens to buy what they produce.
If, on the other hand, production does not increase, or if it decreases, then it is obvious that the money supply cannot increase either; indeed, it must be reduced at the same rate as production decreases. Therefore, we can realize that this is far from the allegations of the former minister of finance, the present member for Toronto-Davenport and Member of the Administration, when he said we wanted to increase the money supply out of all proportions.

The other chief danger arising from excessive expenditures associated with an excessive increase in the money supply-
Mr. Chairman, that phrase "excessive increase in the money supply" is used continuously in the speech of the former minister of finance.
Therefore, it is easy to see that the whole statement of the former minister of finance is based on false premises because the Credi-tistes have never advocated an excessive increase in the money supply. Criticism of a system is always easier after one has inaccurately described it. But if one begins by understanding the exact meaning of Social Credit, criticism becomes more difficult. In fact I have never met anyone yet who could criticize it by stating exactly what is Social Credit. Those people tried to ridicule it rather than understand it.

Because he had said previously:
I do not believe that the proponents of Social Credit feel that price increases and inflation constitute a serious danger.

If the money supply increases unduly, it will lead to price and cost increases and to balance of payments difficulties. If such increases in the money supply and consequent increases in the pressure of expenditures in the economy should persist, we can expect that ultimately it will lead to inflation and, in a country such as ours, to an exchange crisis.
The former minister of finance was waving the spectre of inflation when talking about the Social Crediters.
Well, Mr. Chairman, have we not inflation, today? Is it because of the Social Crediters' theories which are applied. Not at all. They are laughed at. But we are in the midst of inflation, as big an inflation as Canada as never known since the Liberal government came to power. The Social Crediters are not responsible for the present inflation, and still we are smack in the middle of it. What is the cause of inflation? The present government, by continuously increasing taxes, brings about price increases and when prices increase, the workers naturally ask for higher wages and when wages increase, prices increase. But the primary cause, the true cause

March 14, 1967
Bank of Canada Act
of price increases and of the inflation now being felt in Canada is the increased taxes which have been continuously rising since the present government has been in power. That is the cause of inflation. If we are in a period of inflation brought about by a government of which the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) is a member he claims:	"The
Creditistes will bring on inflation." But his own government has brought it about and it continues to worsen. Is there any logic in the criticism of the hon. member for Davenport? None at all, since he is one of the men responsible for the inflation we are now undergoing. And he would blame it on the Creditistes while he has brought it about himself. And he claims:

Well, Mr. Chairman, the Creditistes are not currently in power and applying their theories to Canada. The government is a Liberal one.
Let us look at what that government has done in regard to unfavourable balance of payments of our country.
I have here the latest edition we have received of the Canada Statistical Review, dated February 1967, and on page 70, we shall see what is the balance of payments after three years under a Liberal administration, when during part of that period, the former minister of finance, now Member of the Administration, the hon. member for Davenport, was in office.
In 1965, when the minister made that statement, he had been minister of finance for two years already, what was the Canadian balance of payments? Did it show a surplus? Indeed not. It showed a deficit of $1,083 million at the very time when the former minister of finance was telling us that Social Credit was going to be a danger to our balance of payments.
Are the Canadian citizens to blame? No, Mr. Chairman, because if they had had their say in the matter our balance of payments would have been favourable, since two factors must be considered with regard to the balance of payments: the commodities accounts, that is exports and imports, and the invisible
[Mr. Grcgoire.l
accounts, that is the inflow and outflow of money.
Let us examine the commodities accounts. We worked hard, we produced enough and we exported more than we imported. If one looks only at the commodities account, imports and exports, that is the work done by the people to produce, put on the market goods which are not too expensive, that represents a balance, a surplus of $118 million in the balance of payments. Thus, the Canadian people must not be blamed for the unfavourable balance of payments which showed a total deficit of $1,083 million, in view of the fact that in foreign trade, exports and imports alone, we had a surplus of $118 million.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
But then we come to the invisible accounts, the capital inflow and outflow, because our governments are forced to borrow in New York, London or Belgium, all over the world, because the Bank of Canada does not fulfil its duty, and does not hold sufficient credit to provide for the development of the country. There we see that we have a deficit. So we borrow elsewhere, pay interest rates on foreign loans and end up with a deficit of $1,201 million.
Was a Social Crediter responsible for that? No. The Minister of Finance was in office at the time. He was the one responsible for this deficit in the balance of payments, but he still had the nerve to say: it would be dangerous to accept the Social Credit theories; our balance of payments could be seriously threatened. But it was worse than a threat; at the time the danger not only existed but we showed an unfavourable balance of payments totalling $1,083 million with a deficit of $1,201 million only because our Bank of Canada was not assuming its responsibilities, and our municipal and provincial governments were forced to borrow in the United States, England and sometimes all over the world.
Mr. Chairman, it takes quite a bit of nerve to blame Social Credit theories for the two plagues, the two great calamities of that period, which still exist today, namely an endless inflation and an unfavourable balance of payments unprecedented in our history.
Nevertheless, the former minister of finance said there was no fault or mistake to be found in the monetary system we have today. In fact, he said: I am convinced of the necessity of influencing the money supply to help our economy reach its full potential, at a given
March 14. 1967

time, and to enable it as well to reach a high and constant growth rate.
According to the minister, the handling of money supplies and the regular growth rate were adequate at the time. He felt that that was good and he flattered himself that the expansion was very satisfactory in 1965. Yet, we now realize that the monetary and economic policies implemented by the former minister of finance have led to inflation-of which he is responsible-and restrictions in many fields, in short, they are the cause of the increased unemployment we are now experiencing.
Mr. Chairman, it is all very well to criticize the Social Credit theories, to say that they are nonsensical, that their application would lead us to inflation and create problems in our balance of payments, but we realize that our present monetary system has all those flaws, even though a Liberal government is now in power. We live under this faulty monetary system and the government does nothing to change it and to put an end to the situation.
Mr. Chairman, it is time we found solutions to the problem. It is time to establish a system which will allow the Canadian people to benefit from the wealth of the nation and be prosperous in such a prosperous country.
The subject we have been dealing with, and which I myself had the opportunity of dealing with on several occasions, is that we should like credit to be created by the Bank of Canada rather than by the chartered banks. We are told that money is based on faith. In my opinion, it is somewhat like the minister's answer. I am ready to believe that the minister is not too happy about the way he answered my question and I quote:
-feel and flair-
Maybe a little judgment, to a certain extent, but not too much, because one must not rely too much on the judgment of the Minister of Finance. He stated flatly: I do it by feel and flair and to a certain extent- not too much but some-it remains a question of judgment. But it is mostly feel.
When one asks on what money is based, one is told: On faith. What kind of monetary system is that, Mr. Chairman? Quite an unusual system based on faith, feel, flair and maybe on a little judgment.
Mr. Chairman, Canada should give itself a scientific monetary system, based on reality, on what it represents. In philosophy, Mr. Chairman, smoke is a sign and fire is the significatum. Therefore, if that is applied to money, the sign is the dollar but the significatum is the production. What is the real value of both? It is not the sign, but the significatum. It is the significatum which is the real value, the dollar; money is only a sign which represents, according to the philosophical terms I used earlier, the real value of the country, the real wealth, our production, our ability to produce, our real title. The dollar is only a symbol.
Mr. Chairman, when it comes to evaluating the temperature, the significatum is the temperature; the mercury in the thermometer is only the sign, and the mercury is there only to represent the degree of heat or cold whereas the real value of the temperature is the cold or the heat. The mercury is only a sign which represents the significatum.
Well, Mr. Chairman, if I confine myself to monetary system, our real value, that is the significatum, must be the country's wealth, our output, and the sign must be the dollar, the money supply. However, the sign must give an exact and adequate representation of the significatum. The sign must be a true reproduction of the significatum; otherwise, the sign is broken and diverted from its true role. For instance, if the temperature is-let us say-90 degrees and the thermometer indicates only 8 degrees, it
[Mr. Gregoire.l
will be said that it is out of order, that it is broken and does not represent the true and exact temperature outside, since it is actually 90 degrees, as evidenced by three or four other thermometers, but the other one is broken for it says only 15 degrees. Therefore, the thermometer must be changed.
Similarly, in the monetary system, Canada has a considerable output or wealth. Every last one of us says that Canada is a rich and prosperous country with its oil wells, its wheat production, its ore, its iron, asbestos, copper and nickel mines, its forests that supply lumber throughout Canada and pulp and paper throughout the world, with its tremendous sources of electric power. We have a rich and prosperous country. But because the sign is lacking, the sign which must give a true and adequate representation of the country's wealth, the Canadian citizens are not as prosperous as the country.
Canada is a prosperous country. But because the sign is inadequate, because our monetary system, which is the sign, does not adequately represent the country's riches and prosperity, because that monetary system is like a thermometer that is out of order. As a result, the sign, that is, the dollar, is preventing production from reaching Canadian homes and the Canadian people. The result is a simple one: it can be said that our population is poverty-stricken in a land of plenty.
Our country is one of the richest in the world. But, nevertheless, there are at present, in the province of Quebec alone, 114,000 unemployed who live on meagre unemployment insurance benefits and as many persons in receipt of welfare allowances who do not live, but merely exist with the small weekly or monthly benefits they receive. This is taking place in a so-called prosperous country where the Canadian people are unable to share as they should in the national prosperity, wealth and development.
Mr. Chairman, this points to a deficiency. If our monetary system, which is the sign of our prosperity, is a failure, if it does not represent more adequately the country's wealth and prosperity, it is then up to parliament and to this committee of the whole to study the Bank Act, the Bank of Canada Act, which is the sinew of our monetary system. It behooves us to change this monetary system, to gear it to modem times, to the country's wealth, to the Canadian people,
March 14, 1967

so that this wealth may reach Canadian homes and the Canadian citizens.
This is what is lacking today. Why? In spite of our enormous production, of our tremendous wealth, the fact remains that the sign of that national wealth and prosperity is inadequate since it does not enable the Canadian people to avail themselves of the country's wealth.
Well, then, I say it is up to all of us to consider in depth this Bank of Canada Act which is the main sinew of our economic life, to amend it and change it so that the Canadian people may benefit more from the prosperity of the country.
Some claim that we are infringing upon their privileges by speaking too long. Mr. Chairman, I will say this to those people. We have had the Bank of Canada Act under consideration for two days only. It had not been before parliament in 12 years and the Bank of Canada controls the whole monetary system and the whole life of the country. It is the main sinew of our monetary system and of our whole economic life. Yet, some people find that two days is too long even though some hon. members found means to talk for three months on the Canadian flag. Let no one tell me that two, three or four days, or even two weeks is too long for the members who are present here to analyse the amendments to the Bank of Canada Act.
Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, and I mean unfortunately, I realize there are not enough members elected by the people in this house who are really concerned with the amendments to the Bank of Canada Act. I realize that there are not enough who would study our monetary system and toil over the amendments required to improve the Bank of Canada. Unfortunately, I realize that the Minister of Finance is too steeped in or imbued with the prejudices of the traditional, conservative and orthodox economic system to be in a position to find the solutions to our present economic problems.
Mr. Chairman, time has come to bring about drastic changes to our economic and monetary system if we want Canada to make advances, if we want the Canadian citizens to share in the wealth of Canada, because at the present time-it is a sad thing to say-foreign investors benefit and share much more than the Canadian citizens in the gains derived from the development of our natural resources. Foreign investors get more profit out of our natural wealth than
Bank of Canada Act
our Canadian citizens. Our Canadian citizens work in the woods, in the mine pits while foreign investors reap the benefits. Why? Because we are told that we do not have enough capital to invest in the development of our country. Canada will never really control its economy until the day when it sets up the necessary institutions which will bring in the capital required for the development of our country. Until then we shall keep on trying to administer with the minister's flair and feel-lings, with a little judgment if necessary, but the economy of our country will not make progress that way. What is needed is a scientific and rational system.

Mr. Chairman, it affords me pleasure, after taking a good meal, to proceed with the few remarks I wish to make this evening. I hope that the minister, as well as his parliamentary secretary, have regained their strength, in order, at least, to listen very patiently to what we have to say about the Bank of Canada.
As I was saying before supper, our hopes were renewed last night when we saw the house listen quietly to the remarks of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) and we really hoped at the end of the day that some would understand something about our claims and the cause we are defending. But lo and behold, through some magical power, I suppose, a financial wind swept over that quiet assembly; everything changed and members of the government returned to their old ways and showed as much ignorance as ever.
However, Mr. Chairman, I believe such discussions were useful since, first of all, we succeeded in having the minister express his opinions at various times, but not always.
March 14, 1967

And this will be published in the record. What we are saying today is not so much for this committee but for the record and for those who read it and who want to know what is going on in this house.
We succeeded in having the minister admit that chartered banks actually create money, that they receive deposits from the Bank of Canada, that cost absolutely nothing to them, deposits which they have a right to multiply twelve times and a half and to lend at 8 and 9 per cent.
We wish the government would attribute certain members four, five or six members, small banks like that, which would not be expensive. I believe it would be profitable to multiply them so as not to always grant such a little group the privilege of taking hold of this country's wealth and of impoverishing the rest of this country. But what would be still better and what we are longing for is that the Bank of Canada plays its part. We do not want to upset anything in the financial system; we simply want every organization to play its part.
The Bank of Canada, which is the bank of the Canadian people, should deal with the general public, and the private banks, that is the chartered banks, the credit unions and so on, should operate in the private sector. I think this is perfectly logical, whereas the system we have today is totally illogical. I am surprised to see that people who consider themselves intelligent do not understand this problem or, if they do, refuse to say so-for I am certain that the Minister of Finance and his parliamentary secretary are intelligent enough to understand it. They know very well that if the Bank of Canada were to take over the present functions of the chartered banks with regard to the creation of credit, there would be no more inflation than is created now by the chartered banks with the same means. They are fully aware of that. Only, the minister cannot speak up because, as I said yesterday and tonight before supper, he is prevented by some occult power from being himself and from saying what he thinks, as are also all the other people involved in the present financial system.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
I was rather surprised, four years ago, to hear the director of a chartered bank who was also a member of parliament tell me, as I was having a discussion with him: "My friend, do you think we do not know what you are saying in the House of Commons? Do you think we are not aware of all this?
Bank of Canada Act
And you are 100 per cent right". That is what he told me. I asked him: "Why do you not let the Bank of Canada undertake such operations?" He said: "My friend, I would like to keep my head on my shoulders". That was a serious thing to say. And that is where I saw the power of international finance, which controls not only our country but most of the nations of the world.
We are glad that the Minister of Finance and Receiver General told us several important truths. He had to hide some from us, for he was not in a position to tell us everything. But he should not say, for example, that he is here to look after the interests of the people, when he is here to look after the interests of the trusts. Let him no try to sell us such stories.
Mr. Chairman, yesterday I mentioned some evidence which was put before the finance committee in 1954. Ever since the beginning we have talked a great deal about the present review, the third since the creation of the Bank of Canada.
I was just reading over some most interesting passages, although an attempt was made to hide them from the public at large; they might also prove interesting for the members of the house, but since they seem to be deaf to all truth, I will now put them on record for the benefit of the people.
I was just referring to the words of a former speaker of the House of Commons here, hon. Mr. Macnaughton, who said:
It seems that now, and always, I believe, if we succeeded in controlling credit by changing for instance the cash reserve of chartered banks, we could eventually stabilize our economy and generalize a monetary system which might improve while expanding-
I am convinced that what Mr. Macnaughton had in mind when he said this, was to increase gradually the chartered banks' reserve to bring them to save 100 per cent of liquid assets instead of the usual 8 per cent they accepted at the time on a deposit. Today we are down to an average of 6.6 per cent. I believe that Mr. Macnaughton gave most valuable advice to the committee in an endeavour to improve gradually the control that the Bank of Canada must exert over our whole monetary system.
After such a straightforward statement, can you deny that the only way to control a company, for instance, is to own at least 51 per cent of its shares? On the other hand, is it not ridiculous to talk about control when you hold only 8 or 6.6 per cent?

March 14, 1967
Bank of Canada Act
So Mr. Macnaughton hoped that the Bank of Canada would slowly recover monetary control. I believe that is clearly logical. That is why we claim that we can gain control of banks through the Bank of Canada when we own 100 per cent of the new credits which are the exclusive property of the chartered banks.
The day is yet to come, I think, when the government, through the Bank of Canada, will cease to control only the insignificant reserves of those who control the blood of the nation and will force chartered banks to have larger deposits than the 10 per cent required each year.
Then the banks, as well as caisses populates and other near-banks, will only be authorized to lend to the extent of their actual assets and not on the basis of fictitious accounts. I would refer those who still think we are talking through our hats, to page 158 of that same report, where they will find the answers of Mr. Towers to Mr. Cannon and the proof that bankers do get favours from the Bank of Canada.

Q.-I understand that to make money more readily available you buy government bonds?
A.-Yes.
Q.-I see by your balance sheet dated December 31, 1953 that, apart from government bonds and fixed capital, your assets are only about $90 million?
A.-Yes.
Q.-Supposing that in order to reach a certain objective you had to buy for more than $90 million worth of government bonds, how would you go about paying the amount in excess of $90 million which you would not have and which you had to pay immediately?
A.-In answering this question I might invite the criticism of Mr. Low on the one side and Mr. Macdonnell on the other, for we would pay the additional government bonds by crediting the amount in our books, namely to the deposit account of chartered banks. Whether or not we purchase the bonds from the banks is immaterial, this procedure can be repeated indefinitely.
Q.-Indefinitely. I thought so, but in an emergency would you not simply make a new issue of money? I suppose you would only have to make a book entry and then pay the bonds, thereby increasing the amount of money in circulation?
A.-Any book entry increasing chartered banks' deposits actually constitutes a new money issue.
Q.-That is creating money, is it not?
A.-Yes.
Is that plain enough, Mr. Chairman? Creating money with one stroke of the pen. You see how easy it is for chartered banks to obtain money. Should they lack any, the Bank of Canada will even be so generous as to make deposits for them. Then, the chartered banks will only have to multiply the

said deposit, which did not cost them a penny, to lend the whole amount to the people. It is as simple as that.
But, it is precisely that operation that the financiers have always withheld from the people. And Mr. Cannon continues:
Q.-During your testimony, you said that there is no limit to the amount of money which can be issued at any time?
A.-That is right.
Where is the control of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Chairman? Do you not think that it would be a good thing to set a limit? Here it is the chairman of the committee, mind you -it is the chairman of the committee who comes to the rescue of the governor of the Bank of Canada, short of arguments. Besides, the same thing occurs all through those inquiries, when the big shots are in danger, when the representatives of the people attempt to know more about the limits set by big finance. Listen to the last answer of the chairman of that time.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
We already have fully discussed that matter.
That is the real shield of the present financial myth. The truth must not be revealed. Therefore, what is the part played by that chairman? I ask you. Is he not there to guarantee the freedom to both parties or to provide only the security of the big financiers? It is for you to decide. As for me, I have only read the evidence. It is strange anyway. And the saddest part of it is that these actions from the chairman occur on many occasions. For example, on page 128, when Mr. Tucker was questioning Mr. Towers:
Mr. Towers, you still hesitate at this time to tell us whether it was wise or not on the part of the federal government in the early thirties to deliberately let the deficits accumulate to make up for the purchasing power which was no more in the hands of the people?

That is the final and clever answer from a committee chairman. That is a very intelligent retort for a committee chairman. It is the instruction to transfer everything to history, to hide everything behind the curtain of ignorance.
Which moved Mr. Pouliot, now a senator, to say as shown on page 93 of the report:
I realize that high finance is not within the grasp of the people. We can neither see nor understand it and I would be most interested in obtaining information on the staff of your bank. I would like to know the salary of Mr. Brooks, your doorman? I asked Mr. King and Mr. Abbott and they told me it was not proper to ask such questions.
And the joke goes on, Mr. Chairman. Behind each director lurks an occult force that continues to haunt parliament.
The people responsible for the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks, the Department of Finance, have their secret sessions just like in the times of emperors, and they sit at the same table as the great world financiers.
Sometimes, tips are passed on, sometimes a danger will be forecast and even the Bank of Canada will supply arms to fight the enemy No. 1, the people. Then, it will be decided to take away or give them something more, according to the whims of the financiers. This is called inflation or deflation.
Has anything changed today after 13 years, the last inquiry into the banks dating back to 1954? Not in the least. As for the inquiry, the present chairman seems to have received the same orders as the chairman in 1954 to protect big finance. It seems the briefs which most favour our present financial system are the ones that are discussed. Witnesses are called before the committee who favour the status quo, while those who are hostile to it are almost systematically kept away.
A few are accepted, merely to confirm the rule. I do not know whether the chairman does all this willingly, but on reading the proceedings one gets the feeling that he is somewhat like St. Paul who said: "For the good that I would I do not; but the evil which I would not, that I do".
And the victim, the people, continue to be sacrificed on the altar of the golden calf, big finance. The astounding thing about it, is that we always find in our midst, more and more high priests of big finance to offer the holocaust without uttering a word. A foreboding of this occult course probably moved His Holiness Pope Pius XII to say that those who control money and credit,
Bank of Canada Act
control the blood of the nation, and that without their permission, no one has the right to live.
Mr. Chairman, I wanted to read statements of people who are not socreds. I also want to point out that I could quote, for hours on end, people who, although they do not look upon social credit with favour, still advocate financial reform. For instance, I could name Rev. Father Levesque, one of the great French Canadians, who said:
If you would not have communism nor socialism, then set social credit against them. It alone has the means to check those two perverse movements.
Today, we no longer hear of Father Levesque. He was banished to Africa. That is how I was able-I know the family very well- once again to see first hand that real strength which can neither be seen nor felt, but which stands there watching the interests of big finance. It is a royalty which, it seems, it is very dangerous to attack.
As for us, it may be that we have more gall than the others, but we attack that royalty which is high finance, for we think that if we do not destroy that myth, tomorrow the people will be destroyed. We are here to save the life of the people, Mr. Chairman. I feel all the members should realize that the time has come for the Canadian people to deal with its business seriously, and to see to it that those various organizations fulfil the role for which they were created.
When one considers the Bank of Canada Act, its definition, the first duty it must perform, one finds that this role has been well determined: to control currency and credit 100 per cent. What has caused it to abandon its role? The power of financiers who have bought the representatives at a good price to stop it from doing its duty.
Mr. Chairman, if someone will listen to us once more, we just want the Bank of Canada to create, on behalf of Canada, on behalf of Canadians, new credit and to cease giving for nothing our yearly surpluses to the chartered banks which are private institutions. I do not despise them, far from it, but they have their duties and I say that they are not playing their role at this time. As a matter of fact, they are taking over the role that belongs to the Bank of Canada, and it is imperative that the Bank of Canada should control credit and particularly put it at the service of Canadians and stop the practice of borrowing our own credit.

March 14, 1967
Bank of Canada Act
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Someone was asking me the other day: But, sir, what are we going to do to get rid of those debts that accumulate from year to year?
And I answered: "My dear friend, with the system we have, there is only one way. That is to stop producing, because as soon as we produce, as soon as we have surpluses, we have a new debt the next day. To stop getting into debts, we must stop producing."
Mr. Chairman the more we produce, the more debts we will have. Because it is essentially the basis of our present system, because the Bank of Canada is a debt agency, that has been made quite clear in every report.
Mr. Chairman, I still would have a number of reports to quote, such as, for an example, Hon. Lucien Maynard's brief which is reported on page 318 of the proceedings and evidence of the standing committee of 1954. Hon. Mr. Maynard submitted a marvellous brief in which he gave some definitions, some examples, an historic outline of the banks within our financial system. In the second part of his brief he referred to the faults of our financial system. He also referred to the accumulation of debts as a defect, and he compared our financial system to a poker game.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, it would have been more interesting for all members if they had read these reports once, twice and even ten times, to understand at last the ridicule of our present financial system.

Mr. Chairman, I have
but one question to ask of the Minister of Finance. Up to this point, I have had the opportunity to give some explanation of our ideas on credit creation. I should now like to leave this area. I have put my questions in this regard and I think I have given the long and short of my views. We have the answers of the Minister of Finance recorded in Hansard. We will now let the Canadian public be the judge both of the value of the arguments with regard to credit creation and of the minister's answers. The public will be the judge and will decide who, in these discussions, brought forward useful arguments and suggested amendments to the Bank of Canada Act so that the Canadian people may profit by its monetary system.
The question I should like to put tonight deals with another thing. I have begun to touch upon the subject this afternoon. I refer to the money supply in circulation, to the

volume. As clearly stated by the minister, it is obvious that it is the Bank of Canada which decides what the money supply will be. If the Bank of Canada issues $1,000 in cash, it means that there will be $100 worth of money supply, once the chartered banks have proceeded to the creation of credit. If the Bank of Canada wishes to bring that $100 down to $50, all it has to do is to withdraw $4 from Canada's money supply. On the other hand, should it want to increase the money supply to $150, it will simply add $8 in cash, and then the money supply will jump to $150.
What I would like to know from the minister is this: How does the Bank of Canada proceed to determine what the volume of the money supply should be? On what criterion did the Bank of Canada base itself in 1960, for example, when it enacted that the money supply would be about $12 billion, that it would be $15 billion in 1964, $17,186 million in 1965 and that, at the end of September, 1966, the money supply would be $18,155 million? At least there is an increase. It is not a round figure increase when you add $800 million at a time, or $1 billion, no, that is different from month to month, that can increase by $197 million.
What I would like to know is this: What are the criteria upon which the Bank of Canada bases itself to increase that money supply? Are there any criteria? What are those criteria which are dictated to the Bank of Canada and by which the latter determines, at a given time, the volume of the money supply?
One who receives the monthly reports of the Bank of Canada knows that the money supply fluctuates continuously, from week to week, and that every week, the Bank of Canada buys or sells bonds to keep the money supply in constant fluctuation.
Tonight, I should like to ask the minister the following question: What are the precise criteria the Bank of Canada uses to determine what will be, on a given day, the volume of the money supply in Canada?
I hope that the minister will be able to answer that question immediately.

I shall do my best to reply to these questions of the hon. member for Lapointe whose curiosity is insatiable. May I reply by quoting, first, the statements made by the governor of the Bank of Canada to the royal commission on banking and finance, the Porter commission, in which he put
March 14, 1967

forward the standards he was trying to maintain for the economic and financial welfare of the nation? They are-
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
-sustained economic growth at high levels of employment and efficiency, internal price stability and the maintenance of a sound external financial position, an equitable sharing of economic benefits and burdens and the maintenance of a high degree of economic freedom.

According to statistics which can easily be analysed, each time that the Bank of Canada puts in circulation $2 in cash, one dollar remains in circulation either in the cash registers of stores or in the pockets of the Canadian citizens and the other goes into the vaults of the chartered banks or in their coffers to be used as cash reserve.
Therefore, out of $2 put in circulation by the Bank of Canada, one remains in circulation and the other is used as cash reserve. There are statistics to prove this.
Every time there is a dollar in cash reserves in the coffers or drawers of the chartered banks, these banks can multiply that dollar by 12.5, which gives a money supply of $12.50. This is for each and every dollar.
If we continue to analyze the statistics and examine the cheques exchanged in private offices and the payments made in cash, we realize that each dollar in the money supply, meaning the total credit cash reserves, circulates 25 times in one year.
Each one of these dollars in the money supply, even if it circulates 25 times in one year, represents only $2.50 in purchasing power. To return to my original example, if the Bank of Canada puts $2 into circulation, one of them will go into cash reserves and become $12.50 in money supply, and if you add the other dollar, which remains a part of the cash in circulation, it brings the total to $13.50. These $13.50, after circulating 25 times, will represent a purchasing power of 2.5 times that, which comes to about $33.

However, I draw some satisfaction out of this situation since it will enable me to express my views on the matter.
By the way, I do not forget that ever since I became a member of this house I saw debates last for one month and even a month and a half on matters which were sometimes trivial and contributed to cast a shadow on our members' reputation. And still, almost the whole team was ready to clarify its position on the Munsinger case, for instance, and many others.
When you contemplate a means to tax people, then you have a good turn-up for discussion. But when you are looking for a system which would enable Canadians to enjoy a decent way of life, members who are ready to take part in the debate are much less numerous.
It surprises me that after so many years of study and after thousands of opportunities to realize that the real source of most of the problems is a financial one, we now seem to urge the passing of a bill, which, in my opinion, does not constitute a very constructive contribution since it provides for few changes with this exception that it allows for a greater control of the financial system over the economic activities of the country.
It is reasonable to believe that the monetary system of a country should be a public service operated in the public interest. It is inconceivable that one or two private enterprises can control the amount of money in circulation. Under our ill-organized system, the only way to increase the amount of money in circulation is for a bank to make a loan to the government or to an industry by making a simple entry in the credit account of the borrower. But such loans are not in the least based on the country's increased production.

In our modern economy, you need more and more money because of the great discrepancy between labour and money, so there is a surplus of production. Yet, we are faced with a situation where a sizeable percentage of our families find it very difficult to buy food, clothing, lodging and pay for health care. The livelihood of the majority of individuals and families today depends on a salary, and the salary depends on employment. It is obvious that as soon as employment ceases, the salary ceases too. I think that we do not pay enough attention to the real value of things. If there were only banks in the country, banks everywhere, but no farms; bankers but no labourers or farmers, safes in the bank vaults, but not a single bag of flour or potatoes, not a pound of meat, cheese or butter-nobody could live in this country even with banks, it would be impossible to stay here without any food to eat.
Faith in our country, that is the real credit of a nation, comes from those who contribute one way or the other to the production of goods; from those who work, who teach, who create, who raise families and render services.
The base of credit, which is the real value of money, is the production of the country and those are all the factors who contribute to maintain or increase production.
Those factors are found in organized society, in the means of production but not in the banks.
All members of a society, considering the organization of life in society, enable us to receive from others and to give to others; therefore, the real credit of a country is an eminently social credit.

Besides, it is on that same credit the provinces and nations have been accustomed to sign debentures which they ask bankers to transform into credit money.
Unfortunately, as soon as banks have transformed that credit into credit money, for governments or for industrialists, bankers look upon it as if it were their own. They lend it and keep the debentures, the borrowers' promissory notes as a guarantee, giving them the right to take hold of the very basis of credit, the means of production, should the borrowers not repay the bankers, with profit, the credit the producers have built, but which the banker has only put into circulation.
We feel this is prostituting the credit of this country and turning it into a debt which burdens our economy.
How is it that the government orders through its legislation, to the officials of the income tax, to deduct from the worker's salary this or that amount and that it does not seem to be able to order a few holders of bank charters to create credit in accordance with the actual wealth? How is it that the government of this country continues to yield to the requirements of the financial system; a government supposed to lead, has become the flunkey of private interests.

This power becomes particularly irresistible when exercised by those who, because they hold and control money, are able also to govern credit and determine its allotment, for that reason supplying so to speak, the life-blood to the entire economic body-

Nothing prevents a country which so desires to balance the purchasing power of the people with the domestic production or with imports from other countries in exchange for our surpluses.

It is an integral part of the banking principles and operations of every country in the world, including the United States, Great Britain, France, etc. However, I shall confine my remarks to the situation in Canada because the committee was asked to examine the Canadian banking legislation and its effects on the economy of the country.
The chief disadvantage or weak point of the Canadian banking system arises from the effect it has of piling on the shoulders of the Canadian citizens a constantly increasing load of debt that can never be paid off.
March 14, 1967

As I have previously explained, ithe first charters originally gave the banks the power to issue notes to the extent of three times the cash on hand. You will recall that the banks were required to remit in kind all the notes issued. Some banks succeeded in doing this and they are still operating. Others failed because they were not able to meet this condition. You will find on pages 782 and 783 of the proceedings of this committee a table showing what happened to the 110 chartered banks that have operated or were incorporated since confederation.
Only eleven are still in business.
There are now eight and there will soon be ten, because two new bank charters have been granted.
I will read further:
Profits made by banks are especially the result of interest charged on loans. At the beginning, profits were small, simply because loans were based on the figure of fiduciary circulation, restricted itself to three times the share capital paid in addition to the bank cash deposits. Nowadays however, profits are higher, because banks are free to grant some loans under the form of bank credit up to 20 times the amount of legal tender on deposit. In fact, they seldom exceed the ratio of 10 to 1.
Mr. Chairman, a few years ago, during one of the first federal-provincial conference, that is in 1942, a former Conservative leader, who was then premier of Manitoba, Hon. John Bracken, stated at that conference that the present tax source was unbalanced.
As for the interest which I mentioned earlier, it must be understood that the Canadian workers will pay taxes to provide the necessary money for the interest on the national debt.
And this is what led John Bracken to declare in 1942:
The unbalanced tax system transfers the income of comparatively low-wage earners to those who have comparatively higher incomes. The proceeds of indirect taxes collected by the federal government are mostly used to pay the interest on the national debt-
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I would like to ask the minister how he intends to reimburse the present debt of Canada. Only a few days ago, my colleague, the member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin), put on the order paper question No. 2,485, which was answered on March 13, last, as shown on page 13879 of Hansard.
How many years will it take the government of Canada to reimburse the debts it has been accumulating since 1867?
Bank of Canada Act
Here is the reply given by Minister of Finance:
The government of Canada's outstanding debt represents the cumulative total of all government cash deficits less surpluses since 1867. The deficits, have been financed through the sale of cash; securities while surpluses have been used to reduce-the total of securities outstanding. Changes in debt for any period of time, assuming a constant, cash balance, represent the difference between government cash receipts and expenditures of all kinds-and are, therefore, the consequence of the government's fiscal operations. Since these fiscal operations have a very important effect upon Canada's economy, fiscal policy must take into account prevailing economic circumstances and the probable consequences of any action taken.
That is only part of the minister's answer. At this point, I would like to ask him who determines what the prevailing economic circumstances are in Canada. And I quote the end of his answer on that occasion:
It is not possible to predict when economic circumstances would make it appropriate for fiscal policy to aim at achieving cash surpluses. It is* therefore, not possible to forecast whether or to what extent the government would consider it appropriate to reduce or eliminate all its outstanding debt.
So, Mr. Chairman, it seems that the minister does not know how and when we will be able to repay this debt which now costs us over $1,200 million per year.
I am very much concerned about the answer given by the minister, Mr. Chairman, and I will put again the question to him. When and how will he manage to pay that debt, so that the Canadian taxpayer, the Canadian worker, will not have to pay that interest which goes directly to those who hold claims on Canada's debt and who are not farmers or workers or settlers, but who are well off and few in numbers.
I hope the minister will come up with a satisfactory answer. If he does not want to accept the Social Credit policy, let him find another one, at least, let him get us out of the economic mess we are in.

If I remember correctly-and the hon. Minister of Finance can give us precise information on this subject-the Bank of Canada did lend money to our provinces during two years, from 1934 to 1936 but, according to statistics, it has not lent any money directly to the provincial governments.
In my opinion, this is an anomaly, and it is obvious that this important body, this financial and monetary nerve centre does not answer the needs of the provincial governments. The latter are often forced to borrow on foreign markets at excessive rates.
I remember, for example, a very dynamic and necessary event which occurred in the province of Quebec in 1962, when the government of that time decided to nationalize the electric power of the province, which was produced by several private companies, in order to direct and encourage industrial expansion and the development of the natural resources in the province. It was thought important, in the Quebec of 1962, that the state of Quebec should direct the development of the natural resources and the expansion of the industry in the province by owning and controlling the production of electricity in the province. There was a most dynamic and quite justified measure for developing the province of Quebec. In order to meet this provincial requirement, the Quebec government was forced to borrow on the American market $300 million at excessive interest rates, considering the administration costs and the financial position of the province. In such circumstances as well as in all others where requirements of the various provincial governments in this country are involved, the Bank of Canada, this national institution whose prime object should be to serve the Canadian citizens as well as the governments representing the Canadian people-this backbone of our monetary and financial administration, does not adequately meet the needs of

Canadians and of the provincial and other governments in this country.
Mr. Chairman, this suggestion to increase the services provided by the Bank of Canada to the Canadian people, to the provincial as well as the municipal governments and to the school boards, as the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) has proposed, is most timely. It goes without saying that the Bank of Canada should serve the interest not only of the federal government, but also of the provincial and other governments in this country. It should extend its field of operations. Its constitution of 1934 does not prohibit such an extension and precedents exist to the effect that the bank did make loans from 1934 to 1936.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Obviously, Canada, through this organization that is the Bank of Canada, is even lending money to foreign countries, to foreign banks. I can understand that Canada, in the external affairs field, as well as in international affairs, as far as financial and monetary matters are concerned, cannot live isolated from other countries and other international organizations, such as the International Monetary Fund. Considering certain historic and economic bonds, obviously, the government of Canada has even loaned, in 1964, to the Bank of England a sum of $200 million, I believe, without interest.
This is the service that our Canadian bank renders to foreign countries. But we must not forget that charity begins at home. The first to profit by this intelligent administration by the qualified personnel of this bank and by all the administrative machinery would certainly be the provincial governments and the other governments of this country.
I ask the minister to take into account the claims of many Canadians. I think that a body like the Bank of Canada would have to play a better, more obvious, and very useful role. And this would be an opportunity, among many others, to cement a kind of national unity, not in the realm of feelings, but in the field of the dollar which is very interesting for everybody, for all Canadians, whatever their ethnical origin.
For instance, if British Columbia, Ontario, the Maritimes, Newfoundland and the province of Quebec were to go to the Bank of Canada, managed by the federal government, to borrow the money they need to develop

their provinces and natural resources without always having to go abroad, I am sure they would be very pleased. That would help to draw the various governments closer to one another.
There is a suggestion which is not new. Let us hope to get results along this line.
Mr. Chairman, I want to conclude my brief remarks by also asking the minister and I appeal to him to make these representations to the cabinet, where appointments are concerned to recommend to the board of directors, to the governor of the Bank of Canada, to appoint more French Canadians at the top management of this bank.

These figures are reported at page 18 of a booklet I wrote in 1963 and which is entitled: "The Last Chance". Here is what it says:
At the Bank of Canada, out of a total of 12 high officials, only one was a French Canadian.
I am sure that the minister is convinced that there are now many competent French Canadians in business, in monetary and administrative matters. Some French Canadians have proved themselves in the field of management and hold high administrative posts in the most important chartered banks in the country. We even have French Canadians who have spent sometime with chartered banks outside Canada, who have acquired the best experience at the administrative, financial and monetary levels.
Again that would be an opportunity to strengthen national understanding and unity.
In this centennial year, should there be any vacancies within a few weeks or months, some French Canadians could be added to the high officials of the Bank of Canada. It is not only a sociological matter, Mr. Chairman.
If a French Canadian was appointed to a high post it would enable those who direct the monetary and even financial policy of this country to understand better the aspirations of the province of Quebec which are not revolutionary but evolutionary. Quebec wants to play its role in Canada; it wants its fair share in every field. In the financial field, in the borrowing field, in the Bank of Canada, in the monetary field, Quebec wants to make a contribution. It would like to make suggestions,
Bank of Canada Act
and French Canadians would even like to be consulted.
As the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau) pointed out quite recently, French Canadians must think of asserting themselves competitively in our country, but before we can do so, we must be provided with opportunities to participate in a fair competition. In many fields, especially with regard to higher positions in the Bank of Canada, French Canadians have not been allowed to compete, as pointed out recently by the hon. member for Mount Royal before the members of the Canadian Club in Montreal.
If we are to compete, some of our compatriots must be appointed and there are many of them. The minister knows who they are, as well as the hon. member for Mount Royal and other government members. Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to speak at great length, as I do not want to delay the passing of this bill tonight. If the government wishes to continue a few minutes after ten o'clock in order to pass this bill, we will not object. We want to show that our part in this discussion is not obstruction, but we participate therein so as to express our point of view.
If the minister wants to have this bill passed tonight, we would have no objection to sitting for ten or fifteen minutes after ten o'clock. We believe that the whole bill could be passed by that time.
Mr. Chairman, I would simply like to summarize our position in the course of the debate that took place yesterday and today as regards the amendments to the Bank of Canada Act.
We regret that the government did not see fit to consider, analyse and take into account the suggestions we made in order to bring a few improvements to the Bank of Canada Act.
Our suggestions, the improvements we are suggesting pertain to two areas. First, we have expressed the wish that the Bank of Canada should create credit, instead of the chartered banks. We feel that money is credit. This is the most important factor, the factor which is most essential to the economic development of a country. We do not think that

March 14, 1967
Bank of Canada Act
the creation of credit and money should be left in the hands of the chartered banks which are private enterprises and which have this exclusive privilege and who use this creation of credit for their own purposes. Now, the chartered banks create credit, as the minister himself admitted it.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
We do not want this creation of credit left to some large chartered banks who would use it not for the benefit of the population as a whole, but for their own interest, for their own benefit.
At the same time, if this creation of credit were put under the control or in the hands of the Bank of Canada, this crown agency would not act in its own interest or for the benefit of some big capitalists; to the contrary, it would act in the public interest and for the benefit of every Canadian. This is the fundamental difference.
A state bank like the Bank of Canada should control and regulate itself the creation of credit in favour of the population of Canada, whereas actually the private banks, that is the chartered banks do so to their own benefit and in their own interest whenever they can.
We are against this, because creation of credit is probably and certainly the most important factor of our economic life.
Second, we have asked the government and the minister which criteria the Bank of Canada and the government itself use to determine the money supply. It is useless to say that we were not satisfied with the replies given, since everything is run in a haphazard way, without any directives and there is nothing really scientific which would serve to determine the money supply which is needed.
To us, this is very important because upon the amount of money supply will depend the economical expansion of the country, the buoyancy of the country as well as the prosperity of every Canadian.
Mr. Chairman, it is unfortunate that the minister and his government chose not to take into consideration those two determining factors in our growing Canadian economy. It is regrettable. We believe the Minister of Finance should have taken those suggestions into serious consideration, because the objective here is to enable every Canadian citizen to live decently, honourably, with dignity and

liberty and to enjoy security in a country fabulously wealthy, capable of ensuring that each and every one living here can live decently and honourably.
If the minister is bent on holding up our system to ridicule, well, let him find another one under which can be achieved the objectives for which any economic system is established, that is to ensure that all Canadian citizens can live decently, honourably and with dignity. That is what we expect from our Canadian economy. We have had one opportunity since yesterday-for the first time in 12 years to express those ideas to the government. It chose to ignore them, not to act on them. We are sorry about that. Now, it will be up to the Canadian people, to the people of Quebec to pass judgment on the attitude of the minister, on the policy of the government in that field. The people will continue to ask: what is the use of having a prosperous country if that prosperity is not reflected in fact in the lives of its citizens? What is the use of having such bounteous natural resources in Canada, if Canadian citizens can not share them and benefit from them? That is what we would like to achieve through our suggestions to the Minister of Finance.
We regret that these suggestions have not been heard. We shall let the people judge and they will be capable of deciding whether it is normal, logical and reasonable to live poorly in such a rich and prosperous country. What would bring this prosperity in our Canadian homes would be an adequate economic and monetary system. But there are some who do not want our monetary system to be adequate. They tell the Canadian people: keep on bearing it and living in misery in the midst of plenty.
It is now for the Canadian people to judge the minister and the present government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) if he had received a telegram from the operators of our grain elevators and from the municipal council of Trois-Rivieres objecting to the increase in fees on the St. Lawrence seaway and the Welland canal.
The minister said he had received no telegram. I understood why, a few minutes later, because while questions were being asked here, which, to my mind, were not important, I took time oft to go through the papers and I realized that the minister had just stated that there would be no increase.
So I immediately called those people, my municipal council and the directors to tell them: If the telegram has not gone, do not bother sending it because it seems that the problem is settled. I have here the telegram, the original telegram reporting that the municipal council of Trois-Rivieres strongly objected to the increase in fees on the seaway as likely to be detrimental to the economy of the whole Trois-Rivieres area.
But I would nevertheless like to take this opportunity-and I thank the minister for his intervention to prevent such an increase in fee-with your consent, since I realize I am stretching the rules, if ever so slightly, to remind the minister that the grain elevators of Trois-Rivieres are faced with a difficult problem which I would not want to explain all over again since I have already spoken of it. I should simply like to ask the minister whether he could not unofficially and for the good of the economy of the whole area served by the grain elevators to ask the responsible officials of the National Harbours Board to call, again to discuss the matter, an informal meeting with the mayor of Trois-Rivieres, the representative of the grain elevators, the federal member for Trois-Rivieres and the provincial member for Trois-Rivieres, because there is a question of taxes, as the minister is aware, that concerns the provincial area.
I believe that if we could gather around a table these people whom I call men of good will, to talk together, we might find a compromise to a difficult problem which endangers the very existence of our grain elevators, something which would seriously affect the
14012	COMMONS DEBATES	March 14, 1967
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion area. We are also suffering from the effects of progress. You know that my hon. friend from Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) claims that winter navigation does not operate well. I will state, tonight, that it is operating too well and the ships go right up to Montreal and do not stop at Trois-Rivieres. We are therefore victims of progress, and as a matter of fact, for the first time this year, we have almost no ships.
I understand there are other considerations, and that longshoremen are not too anxious about it, but the fact still remains that our harbour facilities and particularly our grain elevators are mortgaged. I would therefore ask the minister if he would first take the initiative of calling this informal, and I mean informal, meeting of all these people of goodwill.
And here I will perhaps encroach more seriously upon the rules of procedure, to remind the minister that he once promised to help me to appeal to the Canadian Pacific to restore the night train between Montreal and Quebec for Expo '67.
I must say to the minister that in spite of the official resolutions of at least 20 or 25 municipalities, in spite of the support of a large number of members of his party, of the opposition and representatives of the provincial governments-the legislature is passing this week a bill in that connection-the authorities of the Canadian Pacific are objecting to that project and deny us that night train when the last train is at 7.30 p.m. It is being claimed we do not have the necessary facilities, whereas we know that the cars are loaned to the Canadian National, which has two more trains on the south shore, a fact that does not help the north shore.
We know that the city of Montreal will not be able to accommodate all visitors to Expo '67. We know that millions of persons between Montreal and Quebec will want to visit Expo '67, will wish to spend the night there and not be obliged to come back at 7:30 in the evening, but rather at midnight as was done in former days when we used to have a train at that hour. We know it is not true that such a service is an uneconomic one, since we have made economic studies on this matter.
Therefore, I remind the hon. minister of the promise he made to me that he would willingly support our claims to the president of the Canadian Pacific. I say to him that in a few days, the mayors of the municipalities concerned, along with some members of this

house and the member of the provincial legislature will call upon the authorities of the Canadian Pacific in order to prove to them by means of figures and arguments, that they have no right to refuse this essential service to the people, that they have no right to say that it is uneconomic. Besides, we will show them that it is economic.
I know how obliging the minister was. I also know how concerned he is with the whole north shore economy which is in serious jeopardy because of this lack of Canadian Pacific service. I will tell the minister that the service offered by the Canadian National is infinitely better than that of the Canadian Pacific on that section of the province of Quebec I am referring to, except that there is no railroad along the north shore of the St. Lawrence that could serve the more important industrial towns.
Then, I shall recapitulate and express thanks to the minister whose intervention prevented increased rates on the seaway. DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS-BRITISH COLUMBIA-PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some considerable period of time, certainly before my entry into federal politics, we have had a great deal of trouble in the northern coastal part of British Columbia in getting adequate consideration from the government for harbour development. My predecessor, the late Mr. Applewhaite, who was respected in this house and at home as well, has told me in discussions I had with him during the time I was a member of the provincial legislature that this matter arose on a number of occasions, but not a great deal of satisfaction was received.
We have now perhaps four general communities in the northern part of British Columbia that lend themselves to proper harbour development, that is the type of harbour development for shipping purposes. I refer to Stewart, Kitimat, Prince Rupert and Bella Coola, all of which have access or will have access to the interior part of the province and would lend themselves to provincial harbour development.
Even in so far as Stewart is concerned, a few years ago we saw the federal government refuse to proceed further with the agreement with the province of British Columbia to build a road under the roads to resources program which would connect Stewart with the northern hinterland of the province, and the Yukon Territory. If the road had been provided, under a joint program, it would have put Stewart in the business of being a deep sea port. Just the day before yesterday, I believe it was, a bill was introduced in the British Columbia legislature to establish a provincial harbours board. This act would be called the provincial harbours board act.
The purpose of the harbours board, as I learned from a telephone call, would be to develop and to encourage the development of harbour facilities in the province, to provide access to and from such harbour facilities and to assist and promote industrial development of the province in conjunction with harbour development. In the last few years, Mr. Speaker, we have perhaps gone into the area of federal-provincial co-operation to an extent far in excess of that which existed before. We have had federal-provincial conferences on a variety of subjects, not only fiscal matters such as used to take place but matters such as fisheries, Indian affairs, and heaven knows what else.
14013
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
We are in an era of federal-provincial conferences and the atmosphere has been right for some three or four years now for provincial governments to gain access to the ear of the federal government and to work out agreeable arrangements with regard to a variety of problems confronting the different sections of the nation. I submit that here is another opportunity for the federal government to take advantage of the spirit of cooperation that exists between federal and provincial governments, because the federal government is involved in the development of harbours and has been for some time. Here is an opportunity for co-operation to the fullest extent possible so that, with respect to the coast of British Columbia, we may get an orderly, planned harbour development program under way that will give the coast of British Columbia an opportunity to develop its full potential in so far as export shipping is concerned. It would provide access to the deep sea ports for the commodities not only of British Columbia but of the prairie provinces as well, to a far greater extent than exists at the moment.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I hope that co-operation will take place and that we will see this unified approach of the federal and provincial governments to the matter of harbour development, now that the provincial government has expressed its desire to get into this field by the introduction of a bill-of which, of course, I do not have full details at the moment-which sets out the concept of harbour development. Naturally I have a prior interest in the northern half of the province, because that is the area that has been neglected.
I was rather taken aback by the eruption of the minister today resulting from the question that I finally got through to him via Mr. Speaker's hands. So, Mr. Speaker, in this regard I say, please do not take steps, as is permissible under the British North America Act, to disallow the legislation and to engage in a full scale war with British Columbia-because after all on this question, Mr. Minister, we are correct.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS-BRITISH COLUMBIA-PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his lesson in etiquette, which comes exceptionally well from him. There is nothing I would welcome more than the co-operation of the government of British Columbia or the government of any other maritime province in the development of our harbours.
When on November 10 last I announced in Vancouver that the boundaries of Vancouver harbour under the jurisdiction of the harbours board would be extended south from the present limits of Vancouver harbour to the international boundary, I had informed the premier of British Columbia before I made the announcement, as a matter of courtesy. He asked me whether we would co-operate with any plans the province had, and I said that as long as they were in the national interest we would be very glad to do so. I gave him that assurance and said that I hoped that the co-operation would be reciprocal.
I also said, Mr. Speaker, that the government intended at once to initiate long term planning for the development of the facilities that would be required for shipping through the lower mainland, when the capacity of Burrard Inlet and the Fraser River ceased to be adequate to meet traffic needs. I pointed out that there was still considerable room for expansion both in Burrard Inlet and in the Fraser River, but that long term planning should not be delayed.
I also pointed out that the harbours board already had under way economic studies designed to forecast the nature and volume of water-borne shipments up to 1976, and trends to 1986. In addition to the economic studies I said that engineering surveys would also be required. Only last week, Mr. Speaker, the government authorized the National Harbours Board to engage the engineering firm of Swan Wooster to work out plans for future port development between Point Grey and the international boundary, taking into account all
DEBATES	March 14, 1967
types of cargo which can be forecast and taking into account as well the existing and future planned development within Burrard Inlet. This study is to include feasibility, economics, engineering and chronology and is to take into account the full findings of the three studies that have been undertaken in the economic field. Swan Wooster were advised yesterday morning that the study had been approved and should be proceeded with at once.
All this planning is, of course, in addition ' to the very large developments that are taking place in the existing port of Vancouver, which is still a long way from being used to full capacity. The lower mainland harbour facilities are alredy handling most of the overseas export traffic of one third of Canada. These harbour facilities are a vital national asset which must and will be developed in the interest of Canada as a whole by the national government, which has the exclusive constitutional responsibility.
Needless to say we will welcome-and I underline this-the co-operation of the provincial and local authorities as well as that of private interests; but co-operation obviously involves consultation and not unilateral action without advance notice by a government which does not have the constitutional responsibility.
With respect to northern British Columbia I think, with the hon. gentleman, that we shall have to make much more use of Prince Rupert, Kitimat, and probably of Bella Coola and Stewart as time goes on. I think it is in Prince Rupert and Kitimat that we should envisage the earliest development. It is clear with its greater proximity to the Orient that the advantages recognized in Prince Rupert when the National Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific railways were built at the beginning of the century, will be realized long before the end of the century. This involves a national obligation which will be discharged by the national government in the interests of the nation. In doing so we shall welcome all the co-operation we can get from the local authorities and from the provincial authorities. We shall welcome the co-operation of all whose interests are concerned.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
